performers: The Griller String Quartet: Sidney Griller and Jack O’Brien, violins; Philip Burton, viola; Colin Hampton, cello
question: What changes when the thanksgiving music returns after each faster episode?
intro: Beethoven’s slow thanksgiving alternates an F-Lydian hymn with D-major episodes marked “feeling new strength”. Each return changes the counterpoint, until the final hymn threads long violin notes through active lower parts. This guide follows the third movement across the full selected archival file.

cues.title: A thanksgiving for four strings
cues.text: Beethoven heads the third movement “Holy song of thanksgiving of a convalescent to the Deity, in the Lydian mode”. Four strings, not voices, present the hymn. Slow statements alternate with faster episodes, and the hymn’s returns change its surrounding counterpoint.
cues.evidence: Own translation of Beethoven’s heading on the viewed score, printed p.173. The report’s opening sustained region precedes the strong 3:34 change. The selected file’s advertised III–IV identity is disputed separately in the dossier.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: F with a raised fourth
cues.text: The Lydian scale here is F–G–A–B–C–D–E. Its B♮, rather than the B♭ of F major, is the distinctive raised fourth. Listen to the intervals around F rather than assuming that a white-note scale must make C the home note.
cues.evidence: The score’s heading, absence of a key signature and F-centred hymn establish the mode. The report often estimates C major because the pitch collection overlaps; that machine label is not adopted as the written tonic.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Chorale and imitative preparation
cues.text: The slow music combines short imitative entries with more chordal hymn phrases. Distinguish those two kinds of writing: separate lines can prepare a phrase before the four players sustain its harmony together.
cues.evidence: Viewed score p.173 shows the imitative opening and longer chorale notes. This is a passage-wide listening instruction, not a timed entrance or an assertion that all four always move together.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: After illness in 1825
cues.text: A serious illness interrupted Beethoven’s work on Op.132 in 1825. The convalescent’s thanksgiving is his own inscription in the score, not a later nickname supplied by a critic. The quartet was completed that July.
cues.evidence: Beethoven-Haus exhibition guide pp.7–8: https://internet.beethoven.de/pdf-sonderausstellung/Beethovens-Streichquartette-Brief-Guide.pdf ; score p.173 supplies the inscription. No retrospective medical diagnosis is asserted.
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: Weight inside a long note
cues.text: A slow phrase can gather force without acquiring many new attacks. Listen for the changing weight of held sounds and for movement in another part beneath them. Sustained harmony is not necessarily static harmony.
cues.evidence: The first slow span has rising relative level around 2:30–2:40 with only 0.4–0.6 detected attacks per second. The observation is about a broad contour, not an identified chord or bow change.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: Listen for new strength
cues.text: The first hymn approaches a change of pace. Beethoven labels the following Andante “feeling new strength”: D major and three-eighth-note bars replace the F-Lydian slow music. The contrast belongs inside the third movement, not between separate movements.
cues.evidence: Score p.173 gives Neue Kraft fühlend, D major and 3/8 after the slow span. The report’s strong 3:34 boundary and higher relative level and brightness at 3:35 support the approaching join.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The first faster episode
cues.text: In the Andante, the phrase moves through short figures in 3/8. D major introduces F♯ and C♯ into a landscape previously defined by the Lydian hymn’s natural notes. Listen for the change of gait as well as the change of harmony.
cues.evidence: The viewed score establishes the D-major Andante. The report changes near 3:34 and gives D-major-compatible estimates from 3:40; this cue lies within that episode, not at an exactly timed first chord.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Ornament above a moving frame
cues.text: The first violin’s ornamental figures sit above accompaniment that has its own short gestures. Separate the decorated line from the rhythmic support. Faster notes can project a singing phrase rather than replacing melody with display.
cues.evidence: Score pp.173–175 shows violin ornamentation and differentiated accompanying parts in the first Andante. The report has more local activity around 4:20–4:50; no particular ornament is assigned to 4:40.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The hymn remains in memory
cues.text: Keep the slow hymn’s phrase shape in mind during the faster episode. Its return will be recognisable even though Beethoven changes the texture around it. The alternation is between two related states of one movement, not a chain of unrelated miniatures.
cues.evidence: The score’s five-span plan is hymn–Andante–hymn–Andante–hymn. The report supports the next change near 5:40; this cue anticipates rather than precisely times it.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The thanksgiving returns
cues.text: The Molto adagio restores the hymn’s natural-note world and broad pacing. This is a return of material, not a literal replay of the opening: different moving parts surround the sustained melody.
cues.evidence: Score p.175 restores common time and the no-signature slow writing. The report’s 5:40 boundary accompanies lower relative level and brightness, followed by the earlier natural-note pitch collection. Return placement is approximate.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A commission from St Petersburg
cues.text: Prince Nikolai Galitzin asked Beethoven for “one, two or three” quartets in November 1822. Op.132 was one of the three that resulted, alongside Op.127 and Op.130. The thanksgiving therefore belongs within a commissioned chamber work, not a separately commissioned church piece.
cues.evidence: Beethoven-Haus guide pp.6–8 documents Galitzin’s letter and the three commissioned quartets: https://internet.beethoven.de/pdf-sonderausstellung/Beethovens-Streichquartette-Brief-Guide.pdf ; the quoted phrase is attributed to that November1822 request.
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: A familiar line, changed surroundings
cues.text: Listen for a sustained melodic note while another player moves beneath it. The return preserves the hymn’s identity but alters the relationships between the four parts. Similar melody does not require identical accompaniment.
cues.evidence: The first slow return on score p.175 changes the surrounding parts. No specific internal entry or exact repeated bar is claimed at 7:20.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Making the performing parts
cues.text: The professional copyist Wenzel Rampl declined the difficult transcription of the autograph. Joseph Linke and Karl Holz helped prepare the performing parts, which Beethoven corrected carefully. Before listeners confronted the music, musicians had to turn its densely worked manuscript into usable pages.
cues.evidence: Beethoven-Haus guide pp.7–8 describes Rampl, Linke, Holz and Beethoven’s corrections: https://internet.beethoven.de/pdf-sonderausstellung/Beethovens-Streichquartette-Brief-Guide.pdf
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: A mode needs a centre
cues.text: F Lydian and C major share their seven natural notes, but they do not give those notes the same jobs. Listen for where the phrases settle and which bass notes support those arrivals; a pitch collection alone does not identify the tonal centre.
cues.evidence: The written Lydian designation and F-centred phrase structure come from the score. This explains why the report’s repeated C-major estimates cannot determine the movement’s mode.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Renewed strength returns
cues.text: The second Andante restores D major and 3/8. Recognise the faster episode’s family resemblance, then listen for its more elaborate surface. Beethoven revisits the contrast without simply replaying the earlier pages unchanged.
cues.evidence: Score pp.175–178 gives the second Andante and altered figuration. The report has a strong 9:18 boundary, increased relative level at 9:20 and D-major-compatible estimates at 9:25–9:45.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Small notes animate the line
cues.text: In the returning Andante, ornaments and short figures animate the violin writing. Keep the larger phrase distinct from those smaller motions: the episode’s recognisable shape persists through its decoration.
cues.evidence: The second Andante’s elaborated violin line is visible on score pp.176–178. The report gives increased attack activity around 10:05–10:30, including 4.2 per second at 10:10; no individual trill or turn is timed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: An LP date, not a session
cues.text: The Archive catalogues this London Records LP as a 1952 publication; its sleeve carries a 1951 copyright notice. Neither supplies a recording-session date. The photographed labels name Sidney Griller, Jack O’Brien, Philip Burton and Colin Hampton as the four players.
cues.evidence: Catalogue: https://archive.org/details/lp_beethoven-string-quartet-no-15-in-a-minor_the-griller-string-quartet ; viewed sleeve and labels are linked in the dossier. The two year statements describe different kinds of evidence.
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: With the most inward feeling
cues.text: The final slow return is marked “Mit innigster Empfindung” — with the most inward feeling. The hymn returns for the third time, but its long notes now coexist with more elaborate counterpoint. The last return is an expansion, not a bare reprise.
cues.evidence: Own translation of the heading on score p.178. The report’s 11:26 boundary follows the second Andante and introduces lower relative level, lower brightness and sustained slow activity. Placement near 11:26 is approximate.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Long notes, active lower parts
cues.text: The first violin carries extended hymn notes while the other instruments weave more active lines around them. Listen to one of those lower strands without losing the slower melodic span above it.
cues.evidence: Viewed score p.178 shows sustained first-violin notes against moving second-violin, viola and cello parts. This is the final slow region after the report’s 11:26 change, not an exact instrument entrance.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Four strands, not four choirs
cues.text: There is one player on each written part. Try tracing the viola or second violin through a phrase rather than hearing the quartet as a single chordal block. Independent motion gives the final hymn much of its changing density.
cues.evidence: The public-domain score specifies two violins, viola and cello; pp.178–179 shows the final slow span’s independent lines. No enlarged string arrangement is inferred from the collective sound.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A change within the final hymn
cues.text: The final slow span contains contrasts of intensity and texture without returning to the faster Andante. Keep the long hymn in mind through those local changes; a substantial shift in sound need not start another formal section.
cues.evidence: Strong report changes at 13:24 and 13:28 lead to lower relative-level windows at 13:30–13:40, but the sustained final slow region continues. The score places no further Andante after its third Molto adagio.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: Sacred words, instrumental music
cues.text: Beethoven’s heading describes a thanksgiving, but no text is sung. Follow the instrumental phrase lengths and contrapuntal entries rather than expecting a sequence of verses. The chorale-like writing supplies the connection to a hymn.
cues.evidence: The heading and exclusively instrumental scoring are visible on pp.173–179. No identification with a pre-existing liturgical melody or a particular religious service is asserted.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Listeners asked for repeated hearings
cues.text: A Leipzig review in December 1825 praised the quartet’s originality while saying that it required repeated hearing and study. The same account questioned the length of the Adagio and its unusual Lydian notes. Early reception included specific musical objections, not simply unanimous rejection.
cues.evidence: The documentary history cites Allgemeine musikalische Zeitung, 21 December1825, cols.840f, and summarises these reactions: https://www.lvbeethoven.org/opus132/ ; no unsupported claim about all première listeners is made.
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: A slow span can swell
cues.text: The final hymn develops a large contour while keeping its slow pace. Listen for the difference between stronger sustained sound and a faster beat. The melody’s long values remain meaningful even when the surrounding counterpoint becomes more insistent.
cues.evidence: Score pp.178–179 retains Molto adagio through the final span. The report identifies 14:35 among its highest relative-level windows and continues with very low detected attack rates; the cue does not translate level directly into a written dynamic.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Follow delayed resolutions
cues.text: When one part holds a note and another moves, listen for the resulting tension to resolve. Those delayed resolutions connect the slow phrases across their long note values; silence is not the only way to punctuate them.
cues.evidence: The final hymn score contains sustained notes against moving contrapuntal parts. No particular dissonance or resolution is assigned to 16:00.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Private hearings before public concerts
cues.text: Op.132 received private hearings in Vienna in September 1825 before its November public performances. The British musician George Smart attended a September hearing. The work’s first reception therefore included musicians studying it in a smaller setting before the public reviews appeared.
cues.evidence: The documentary account gives the 9 and 11 September private hearings, Smart’s presence and November public performances: https://www.lvbeethoven.org/opus132/
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: The hymn approaches its close
cues.text: The last slow passage settles towards the hymn’s F-centred ending. Listen for how the active lines give way to longer closing sounds rather than expecting one more episode of renewed strength.
cues.evidence: Score p.179 closes III on F after the final hymn. The report shows a late level rise at 17:30 followed by a 17:38 change and a quieter ending region. No new march is established in the selected file; its combined title remains disputed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Allow the final sound
cues.text: The final page of the thanksgiving settles on F. Follow the held ending through its release instead of treating the last moving figure as the end. This guide preserves the selected file’s full duration rather than cutting the slow movement to an excerpt.
cues.evidence: Score p.179 supplies the F close. The report’s final windows have declining relative level and F among the prominent classes at 17:50–18:05; supplementary upper-band inspection is strongly F-centred. File duration is 1092.6 seconds; the exact end of the played release is not established.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: F Lydian gives way to D major
transitions.how: The first hymn reaches held F-centred punctuation. Beethoven then changes the tempo to Andante, the metre from common time to 3/8 and the key signature to D major. F♯ and C♯ replace the earlier natural-note setting; the shared pitch A does not make the shift a demonstrated pivot-chord modulation. Short violin figures and a more active accompaniment replace the broad chorale. The score’s heading, Neue Kraft fühlend, names the contrast within the same movement.
transitions.evidence: Viewed score p.173 supplies the entire written join. The report’s strong 3:34 boundary is followed by higher relative level and brightness at 3:35 and D-major-compatible estimates at 3:40. The locator is approximate, not an aligned first D-major chord.

transitions.title: The slower hymn returns with changed parts
transitions.how: The first Andante quietens towards its close, then the two-sharp signature is cancelled and common time returns. The Molto adagio restores the F-Lydian hymn, but the instrumental parts do not reproduce the opening page literally. Moving inner and lower lines introduce and surround the long melody. The joint return of pace, metre and modal setting makes the material recognisable while the changed counterpoint distinguishes it from a mechanical repeat.
transitions.evidence: Score p.175 shows the quiet Andante ending and slow return. The report gives a 5:40 boundary with lower relative level and brightness and a return to the earlier natural-note collection. No exact part-entry seconds or played repeat count are claimed.

transitions.title: The faster episode returns more elaborately
transitions.how: The second hymn statement again releases into D-major Andante music in 3/8. The contrast in tempo and modal setting recalls the first alternation, while more elaborate figures change the new episode’s surface. Four players remain throughout: the sense of renewed motion comes from their note lengths, articulation and divided functions, not from adding another instrumental group.
transitions.evidence: Score pp.175–176 supplies the second Andante and its altered writing. The report has a strong 9:18 boundary, a relative-level rise at 9:20 and D-major-compatible estimates at 9:25–9:45. Approximate passage placement, not a bar-aligned first attack.

transitions.title: The last return deepens the counterpoint
transitions.how: The second Andante subsides and the final Molto adagio restores common time and the hymn’s natural-note setting. Beethoven adds Mit innigster Empfindung above this return. Long first-violin notes coexist with moving second violin, viola and cello; the hymn’s identity is preserved through a denser network of lines. No further faster episode follows in the written third movement, so this return carries its extended closing span.
transitions.evidence: Viewed score p.178 supplies the instruction and expanded contrapuntal texture. The report’s 11:26 boundary coincides with falling relative level and brightness; the following long region remains slow. No IV boundary is inferred from later novelty peaks.

source.title: Beethoven, Op.132 — Breitkopf & Härtel, Beethovens Werke, 1863, plate B.51
source.locator: Viewed public-domain original quartet score, printed pp.173–179, movement III. One player per token: first violin, second violin, viola, cello. Rows describe broad passage participation and written prominence, not every instant of sound or an audio-separated instrument. The source’s combined III–IV track label is disputed; no IV map is invented.

timeline.note: First hymn, p.173: imitative entries accumulate into four-part chorale writing. The row covers the passage, not simultaneous activity at every opening instant.
First Andante, pp.173–175: first-violin ornamentation over differentiated lower parts; all four contribute across the episode. Approximate 3:34 change.
First hymn return, p.175: moving inner and lower parts surround sustained melody. This is not a claim that the original four entries recur at identical intervals.
Second Andante, pp.175–178: more elaborate violin figuration and active accompaniment. Exact pizzicato or ornament entrances are not timed.
Final hymn, pp.178–179: long first-violin hymn notes coexist with independent motion in the other three parts. All remain participants in the closing F-centred writing.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Original quartet scoring; movement III. The Archive’s combined III–IV designation is disputed.
fields.note: The exact selected 1092.62-second MP3 is retained without truncation or substitution. Its analysed structure supports the five alternating spans of III, at approximately 0, 214, 340, 558 and 686 seconds, followed by slow music through the endpoint. The required report does not establish an A-major march or the IV–V link. Supplementary upper-band inspection finds an F-centred ending; verifier VerH independently checked the selected file’s final37.6s against the score and also found the F ending of III, not IV’s dominant recitative. These are score/audio-feature correspondences, not an aural or complete bar-aligned certification. No IV boundary or IV listening prose is invented. Performing edition, cuts, repeat observance and the completeness of the final played release remain unestablished.

III only, supported by the selected file’s five-span design and independently checked F-centred endpoint

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Territorial EU public-domain basis only: the recording was published before 1963; US status is not established.
fields.note: The admitted basis is eu-published-before-1963, using the Archive’s 1952 catalogue date for this identified London LLP318 issue. The printed sleeve carries a 1951 copyright notice, corroborating an early-1950s package but not independently establishing the first publication year of the sound recording. A recording published by 1952 had exhausted the ordinary EU 50-year phonogram term before 1 November 2013; the 2011 extension applies to recordings still protected on that date. This is territorial, not a Creative Commons grant or worldwide clearance. The US 1947–1956 term is longer, and no US public-domain claim is made. The Archive item supplies no separate recording licence; availability online and Beethoven’s public-domain composition are not the admission basis.

composer.epithet: A pianist who turned small rhythmic cells into long arguments, then rebuilt the forms that contained them.
facts: Christian Gottlob Neefe in Bonn; Haydn, Johann Georg Albrechtsberger and Antonio Salieri in Vienna
Bonn until 1792 · Vienna and its surrounding villages thereafter
Nine symphonies · five numbered piano concertos · 32 numbered piano sonatas · 16 string quartets · one opera
Progressive hearing loss documented in letters from 1801; conversation books used from 1818
composer.background:
Beethoven was born in Bonn in 1770, probably on 16 December, and baptised on 17 December. His father Johann sang in the electoral court chapel, and his grandfather Ludwig had been its Kapellmeister. The family name came from the Low Countries; the ‘van’ did not indicate nobility. Johann attempted to present his son as a child prodigy, but Beethoven’s more substantial training came from Christian Gottlob Neefe, who introduced him to Bach’s keyboard music and helped him obtain work as an organist. Playing viola in the court orchestra also gave him practical knowledge of instrumental and operatic repertory.

The Bonn years supplied more than a musical apprenticeship. The court of Elector Maximilian Franz, educated patrons and friends such as the Breuning family brought Beethoven into contact with Enlightenment literature and social ideas. After his mother’s death in 1787 and his father’s worsening incapacity, he assumed increasing responsibility for the household. In 1792 he left for Vienna to study with Haydn. The intended period of further training became permanent residence: the French occupation of Bonn in 1794 ended the old electoral establishment to which he might have returned.
